name: AveryDay
summary: A habit tracker for self-learners that installs on your phone like an app.
decision: Streaks and progress are calculated from your check-ins every time, never stored, so they can never be wrong.
stack: Spring Boot 4, PostgreSQL, Flyway, Testcontainers, React
imageAlt: The AveryDay dashboard with completion rates and goals
caption: The dashboard running locally with a demo account.

meta.role: Sole developer: backend, frontend and deployment
meta.stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 4, Spring MVC, JPA, PostgreSQL, Flyway, React
meta.status: In public beta. It runs on free hosting, so the first load can take a few seconds.

problem: Most habit trackers are not built for learning. They don’t connect a habit to the goal behind it, and their streaks are either so strict that one missed day ruins them or so loose that they mean nothing.
users: Self-learners and developers who set a goal, such as learning a new language in 60 days, and check in every day. The app is in public beta.
built: Goals with linked habits, notes and study resources.
Habits to build or to quit, on daily, weekday or weekly schedules.
Streaks, XP, levels and a dashboard of completion rates.
Rest days with a weekly limit, and push notification reminders.
Google sign-in, an admin panel, and an installable web app.

architecture.intro: A single Spring Boot application organised by feature. Features talk to each other only through their services, never through another feature’s repository. Flyway manages every database change.
architecture.label: How a session is kept safe

steps.label: Refresh
steps.text: When the short-lived access token expires, the web app asks for a new one. Several requests at once share a single refresh.

steps.label: Cookie
steps.text: The refresh token is kept in a secure, HTTP-only cookie, so JavaScript on the page can never read it.

steps.label: Hash
steps.text: The server stores only a hash of the token, so even a database leak would not expose anyone’s session.

steps.label: Reuse
steps.text: If an old token is ever used again, it is treated as theft and every session for that user is signed out.

steps.label: Rotate
steps.text: Otherwise the token is replaced with a new one and a fresh 15-minute access token is issued.

decisions.title: Calculate progress, don’t store it
decisions.body: Streaks, statistics, XP and goal progress are all calculated from check-ins when they are requested. Nothing is stored that could fall out of sync with the history.

decisions.title: Past days follow the rules of that day
decisions.body: A day counts as complete if it met the target that applied on that day. Raising a target later never changes your past results. Changing a schedule starts a new streak but keeps your XP.

decisions.title: Other people’s data simply does not exist
decisions.body: Every query is filtered by the signed-in user. If you request someone else’s habit, you get “not found”, which reveals nothing about whether it exists.

solved.before: Adding Google sign-in created a subtle security risk called account pre-hijacking. Someone could register with your email address and a password before you ever signed in with Google, and keep access to the account. Now, when a Google account is linked to an account whose email was never verified, that account’s password and sessions are removed. This integration test proves it:
solved.after: Google sign-in tokens are verified on the server against Google’s public keys, and a Google account without a verified email is refused.
